Members of the “Ulugh Beg” astronomy club in Samarkand are studying the moons of the planet Jupiter. For convenience, the average distance of each moon from the center of Jupiter is given in units of “Jupiter radius” (R).

1 R is about 71 500 km.

Moon — Average distance from the center of Jupiter (R)
Metis — 1.79
Amalthea — 2.54
Thebe — 3.10
Io — 5.90
Europa — 9.39
Ganymede — 14.97
Callisto — 26.33
Himalia — 160.3
s0006: In order of distance from Jupiter (left to right), not to scale
s0007: Calculate differences of decimals in a table and choose the set of three that fits a model
s0008: For each option, calculate the differences between the distances of neighboring moons and compare them with the two numbers in the model.
s0009: The model in the picture shows the average distances between three moons (the moons are placed in order of distance from Jupiter, from left to right). According to the table, which moons are in the model?
s0015: The distances in the model are the differences between the distances of neighboring moons.

s0023: So the moons in the model are Io, Europa, and Ganymede.

s0025: The Europa–Ganymede gap is 5.58 R, but in the model it is the second gap; the first gap must be 3.49 R, and Ganymede–Callisto is 11.36 R.
s0026: Only the Io–Europa gap (3.49 R) fits, but in the model it is the first gap; Amalthea–Io is 3.36 R.
s0027: The distances in the model are not the numbers in the table themselves, but the differences between the distances of two moons.

s0030: About how many kilometers from the center of Jupiter is Ganymede?
s0036: From the table, we take Ganymede's distance and the ratio of the units.
s0038: We multiply the number of radii by the length of one radius.
s0040: We round the result to the nearest thousand.
s0042: Ganymede is about one million seventy thousand kilometers from Jupiter.

In her math club, Madina made a staircase-shaped pattern from square tiles. Row 1 has 3 tiles, row 2 has 5 tiles, and row 3 has 7 tiles: each new row has 2 more tiles than the one before. In each row, green and yellow tiles alternate; each row starts with a green tile and ends with a green tile.

The picture shows the first 3 rows of the pattern. The pattern continues downward following the same rule.
s0054: Count objects in a picture and express a part of the whole as a percentage
s0055: Count all the tiles in the first 3 rows and the yellow tiles among them, then divide the number of yellow tiles by the total number.
s0056: What percentage of the tiles in the first 3 rows of the pattern are yellow?
s0058: First we add up all the tiles in the three rows.
s0060: The rows have 1, 2, and 3 yellow tiles.
s0061: We divide the number of yellow tiles by the total number of tiles and convert to a percentage.
s0063: Forty percent of the tiles in the first three rows are yellow.
s0064: There are not equal numbers of green and yellow tiles: each row has one more green tile.
s0065: 60 % is the share of green tiles (9 : 15), not yellow tiles.
s0066: 6 : 9 divides the yellow tiles by the green tiles; for a percentage, you need to divide by the total number of tiles.
s0067: To find a percentage, always calculate “part : whole”; here, the whole is the total number of tiles.
s0068: Extend a pattern rule by one row and calculate the new percentage
s0069: Use the rule to find how many tiles and how many yellow tiles row 4 will have, then calculate the percentage for the first 4 rows.
s0070: Madina added row 4 to the pattern. Now what percentage of the tiles in the first 4 rows are yellow (round to the nearest tenth)?
s0072: Each row has 2 more tiles, and one more yellow tile.
s0074: We add the new row to the previous three rows.
s0075: We divide the number of yellow tiles by the total number of tiles and round to the nearest tenth.
s0077: In four rows, the share of yellow tiles is 41.7 percent.
s0078: This is the answer for the first 3 rows only; when row 4 is added, the share changes.
s0079: 58.3 % is the share of green tiles (14 : 24).
s0080: 10 : 14 divides the yellow tiles by the green tiles, not by the total number of tiles.
s0081: When extending the pattern, do not forget to update both numbers: the total number of tiles and the number of yellow tiles.
s0082: Find a relationship that holds for every row of a pattern and use it to justify a general claim
s0083: Compare the numbers of green and yellow tiles in one row and check that this relationship holds for any row.
s0084: Her friend Sardor said: “No matter how many rows are added to the pattern, the share of yellow tiles will always be less than 50 %”. Is Sardor right? Choose the best answer and reason.
s0085: Yes, because in the first 3 rows, 40 % of the tiles are yellow, which is less than 50 %.
s0086: Yes, because each row starts and ends with green and the tiles in between alternate, so each row has one more green tile than yellow tiles.
s0087: No, because as rows are added, the share of yellow tiles keeps growing and will eventually go above 50 %.
s0088: Yes, because the tiles at the ends of each row are green, and the yellow tiles are always on the inside.
s0090: The rows have 3, 5, 7, ... tiles, that is, an odd number.
s0092: Because each row starts and ends with green, there is always one more green tile.
s0093: In each row, yellow < green ⇒ total yellow < total green
s0094: This relationship holds in every row, so it also holds for the totals.
s0096: The share grows, but it never reaches 50 percent.
s0097: Answer: B) Yes — each row has one more green tile
s0098: Sardor is right, and the reason is the relationship in each row.
s0099: You cannot draw a conclusion by looking at just a few rows: the claim is about any number of rows.
s0100: The share does grow (40 %; 41.7 %; 42.9 %), but it never reaches 50 % because each row has fewer yellow tiles.
s0101: Incomplete reasoning: there are also green tiles inside the rows; mentioning only the ends does not prove that there are fewer yellow tiles.
s0102: To justify a claim that something is “always” true, find a rule that holds in every case (in every row).

The district newspaper published this report about a small family guesthouse on the shore of Charvak Reservoir (the report was made up for learning purposes):

“SUMMER SEASON COMES TO A CLOSE
• The guesthouse did not stand empty for a single day during the season.
• On average, 46 guests were welcomed per day.”

Note: the average number of guests per day is the total number of guests in the season divided by the number of days in the season.
s0105: Justify that the mean does not have to be one of the values in a data set
s0106: Think of a small set of numbers whose mean is 46 but which does not include the number 46.
s0107: Is it possible that there was not a single day in the season when exactly 46 guests came to the guesthouse? Choose the best answer and reason.
s0108: No, because if the average is 46, exactly 46 guests must have come on at least one day.
s0109: Yes, because the mean does not have to be one of the numbers: for example, the mean of 40 and 52 is 46, but 46 is not among them.
s0110: Yes, because on some days more than 46 guests came to the guesthouse.
s0111: Yes, because the average is the result of dividing the total number of guests on all days by the number of days.
s0113: First, let's recall how the average is calculated.
s0115: If 40 and 52 guests come on two days, the average is 46.
s0116: There was no day with exactly 46 guests, but the average is still 46.
s0117: Answer: B) Yes — the mean does not have to be in the data set
s0118: So this is possible; one example is enough to prove it.
s0119: There is a counterexample: the mean of 40 and 52 is 46, but there was no day with 46 guests.
s0120: Incomplete reasoning: it does not say that there can be days above the average and days below it, while 46 itself never occurs.
s0121: This only describes how to calculate the average; it does not explain why exactly 46 might never occur.
s0122: To answer “yes” to a question asking “Is it possible?”, one specific example is enough.

The district education department monitored students' participation in sports clubs at 10 schools. The table shows, for 2022, 2023, and 2024, what percentage of each school's total number of students attend a sports club (the data are fictional, for learning purposes).

The schools have different numbers of students: there are both small village schools and large city schools.

School — 2022 (%) — 2023 (%) — 2024 (%)
School 1 — 34.2 — 35.0 — 36.1
School 5 — 41.5 — 40.8 — 39.7
School 7 — 28.4 — 30.9 — 31.6
School 12 — 52.3 — 51.6 — 51.9
School 15 — 22.7 — 22.1 — 22.7
School 18 — 38.9 — 37.2 — 35.8
School 21 — 45.0 — 46.3 — 47.9
School 24 — 30.5 — 32.8 — 33.2
School 27 — 26.1 — 27.4 — 25.0
School 33 — 36.8 — 34.5 — 35.6

You may use a calculator. Change is measured in “percentage points”: for example, going from 30.0 % to 31.5 % is +1.5 percentage points.
s0125: Use table data to set up the needed differences and find the greatest increase, zero change, and the greatest decrease
s0126: For each school, calculate the difference “2024 − 2022”: find the greatest positive result, the result equal to zero, and the smallest negative result.
s0127: From 2022 to 2024 (in percentage points), at which school did the share increase the most, at which school did it not change at all, and at which school did it decrease the most? Choose the correct set of three (increased the most; did not change; decreased the most).
s0133: We calculate the change between the two years for each school.
s0135: The greatest positive difference is at School 7; School 21 has +2.9 and School 24 has +2.7.
s0136: At School 15, the share dropped in 2023 and then came back, so the overall change is zero.
s0138: The greatest decrease is at School 18; School 5 has −1.8.
s0140: The set of three is School 7, School 15, and School 18.
s0141: School 21 grew the most only from 2023 to 2024 (+1.6); over the whole period, School 7 grew more (+3.2 > +2.9).
s0142: At School 12, the change is −0.4: small, but not zero; the change is exactly zero at School 15.
s0143: The difference was taken the wrong way around (2022 − 2024): the signs are reversed, so the increase and decrease have swapped places.
s0144: When calculating a change, always subtract in the order “later year − earlier year”: positive means an increase, negative means a decrease.
s0145: Calculate the average change over two periods and interpret its sign
s0146: For each year, find the average share of the 10 schools (or the average of the changes in each period) and compare them.
s0147: Consider two periods: 2022–2023 and 2023–2024. Which statement about the average change in the share across the 10 schools is correct?
s0148: The average change is negative in both periods.
s0149: The average change is positive in both periods.
s0150: The average change is negative in 2022–2023 and positive in 2023–2024.
s0151: The average change is positive in 2022–2023 and negative in 2023–2024.
s0153: We add the 10 numbers in each year's column and divide by 10.
s0154: In the first period, the average share increased.
s0155: In the second period, the average share also increased, but by less.
s0156: 5 schools decreased, but the average change > 0
s0157: What matters is not the number of schools that decreased, but the sum of the changes.
s0158: Answer: B) positive in both periods
s0159: The correct statement is that the average change is positive in both periods.
s0160: The average share increased in both periods: 35.64 → 35.86 → 35.95.
s0161: In 2022–2023, the share decreased at 5 schools, but the sum of the changes is +2.2, and their average is +0.22, which is positive.
s0162: In 2023–2024, the sum of the changes is also positive (+0.9), so the average change is +0.09.
s0163: Determine the sign of the average change from the sum of the changes, not from how many schools increased or decreased.
s0164: Compare changes over two periods to find the cases where the rate of change differed the most
s0165: For each school, find the changes for 2022–2023 and 2023–2024, then calculate their difference and choose the two with the greatest absolute value.
s0166: At which two schools was the difference between the change in 2022–2023 and the change in 2023–2024 the greatest?
s0172: First we find the change in each period, then the difference between them.
s0174: At School 27, an increase turned into a decrease.
s0176: At School 33, on the other hand, a decrease turned into an increase.
s0178: At the other schools, the absolute value of the difference is much smaller.
s0180: Regardless of sign, the greatest difference is at these two schools.
s0181: Schools 7 and 24 grew the most in the first period, but the difference between the changes in the two periods (−1.8 and −1.9) is not the greatest.
s0182: School 27 is correct, but only negative differences were considered: the difference for School 24 is |−1.9| = 1.9, which is less than School 33's difference of 3.4.
s0183: Only positive differences were considered; the difference for School 15 is +1.2, while School 27's is |−3.7| = 3.7.
s0184: “The greatest change” means the number with the greatest absolute value, regardless of sign: a decrease is also a change.
s0185: Judge which conclusions cannot be drawn from percentage data (when the base amount is unknown)
s0186: Work out what the table shows: shares, not numbers of students. Think about what else you would need to find a number from a share.
s0187: Ms. Nodira said: “In all three years, the number of students attending sports clubs at School 12 was greater than at each of the other 9 schools”. Do the data in the table support this statement? Choose the best answer and reason.
s0188: Yes, because School 12 has the highest percentage in all three years.
s0189: No, because the share at School 12 decreased from 2022 to 2024.
s0190: No, because the table gives only percentages, while the total numbers of students at the schools are unknown and different.
s0191: Yes, because School 12's three-year average percentage is higher than that of the other schools.
s0192: Table shows: share (%), not numbers of students
s0193: First we work out exactly what quantity the table gives.
s0194: Number = share · total students at the school
s0195: To find the number of students who attend, you must know the size of the school.
s0197: Even if a small school has a high percentage, it may have fewer people.
s0198: Answer: C) No — the total numbers of students are unknown
s0199: The table does not support the statement, because the base amounts are not given.
s0200: The highest percentage does not mean the most students: the schools have different numbers of students.
s0201: The decrease is very small (−0.4) and is not a reason to reject the statement; the main problem is that the total numbers of students are unknown.
s0202: An average percentage is also a share; for schools of different sizes, it does not show numbers of students.
s0203: Before comparing percentages, ask “percentage of what?”; if the bases are different, you cannot draw conclusions about numbers.
